videos.title: Midlands Analyst Huddle: Exploring analysis of primary care services, Steven Wyatt - 24/02/2022
videos.description:
Steven Wyatt - exploring analysis of primary care services
 
Steven Wyatt, Head of Research and Policy at the SU, discusses analysis of primary care services.  ICSs will soon be assuming responsibility for commissioning GP services.  Although 10% of the NHS budget is allocated to primary care, novel analyses of the service are few and far between.  Analysts often say that data access is the key constraint.   This session explores opportunities to improve and extend analysis of primary care services.

Summary: 
In the first half of the session, we will be describing summary primary care datasets that are available from public domain websites.  Have we made the most of these datasets?  We will be assessing network member interest in collaborating on projects that use these datasets.
In the second half of the session, we will be discussing record-level primary care datasets: proposed national data flows, research datasets and local solutions.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: ‘Strategies to reduce inequalities in access to planned hospital procedures' - 05/05/22
videos.description:
Steven Wyatt (Head of Research and Policy, Strategy Unit) shares his strategies to reduce inequalities in access to planned hospital procedures (MDSN project)
In last year’s report, ‘Socio-economic inequalities in access to planned hospital care: causes and consequences’, Steven Wyatt and Jake Parsons described how people living in more deprived areas have poorer access to planned hospital care than their more affluent counterparts. These deficits are widespread, substantial, and worsening. In his new report, Steven moves beyond describing and explaining the problem, providing practical support for those keen to address it. The Strategy Unit starts from the premise that inequities are not immutable. Tackling the issue will not be easy, but it is essential if the NHS is to be true to its founding principles. Efforts to date have clearly not been sufficient. Bolder action and more potent interventions are required.

Steven will share with us his approach, key findings and look at how systems can implement the changes needed to reduce inequalities in access to planned hospital procedures.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: Using system dynamics to gain insight into domiciliary care - 14/07/22
videos.description:
Title: Using system dynamics to gain insight into domiciliary care AND the launch of a new system dynamics development programme
    
In the Huddle on 30/06/22  we had an introduction to System Dynamics and an example of how this was used to support capacity planning https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SKf-tGp23Kg
If you’d like to have a go, yourselves, then please do try out this System Dynamics ‘Ready Reckoner’ https://exchange.iseesystems.com/public/dmck/capa-ready-reckoner/index.html which is a simple model structure is to give an introductory insight into how System Dynamics is used to model capacity in health and social care services.

This week’s Huddle is another look at System Dynamics – this time in relation to domiciliary care and we are also going to learn about an exciting opportunity for you as part of a new system dynamics development programme.  

The Strategy Unit and Douglas McKelvie have been working on an exciting project with WM ADASS, the Association of Directors of Adult Social Care Services in the West Midlands to explore the challenges facing domiciliary care and the opportunities that exist to transform and improve the service. If domiciliary care is not provided, then the effects are felt not just by those who need the service, but also by a wide range of aligned health and care services: hospital beds become blocked and care home beds are overrun. “Using system dynamics we have been collaborating with local authorities to develop through iteration a model which gives us a better grip on what the future might hold and how options to address future challenges might perform.”

And in addition, we are going to be learning about the exciting new development programme and opportunities for analysts and others to be part of this.

In the Autumn the Strategy Unit and Douglas McKelvie will be launching a system dynamics development programme, as well as the core programme there will also be the option of enhanced support for some of the ICSs in the region to be part of a pilot in parallel with NHSEI to use system dynamics to tackle system-wide capacity and demand challenges.

MAN Huddle: Associations between some household context factors & emergency hospital use - 28/07/22
videos.description:
28th July 2022 – Latest analysis on the associations between some household context factors & emergency hospital use

Richard Brine https://www.health.org.uk/about-the-health-foundation/our-people/improvement-analytics-unit-iau/richard-brine
and Liz Crellin https://www.linkedin.com/in/elizabeth-crellin-76708238/?originalSubdomain=uk
from the Health Foundation https://www.health.org.uk/
are going to be talking to us about two household context factors that the Improvement Analytics Unit have derived from national routine administrative health data. 
These are:
. living alone, and
. living in a two-person household with someone who is frail.

They have developed the indicators as they believe they can provide important and useful information related to social context when understanding population health and care needs and could be potential proxies for caring responsibilities or risk factors for social isolation.

The session will demonstrate:
. how the context factors were derived using a pseudonymised Unique Property Reference Number (UPRN) variable contained in a minimised version of an NHS England and Improvement dataset, the Master Patient Index, and
. the results of their analysis into whether these household context factors were associated with emergency hospital use (A&E attendances and emergency admissions) in people aged 65 and over (approximately 5m patients). They found that both factors were strongly associated with both higher A&E attendance and emergency hospital admission, even after adjusting for common predictors of emergency use (age, gender, ethnicity, geographic region, level of socio-economic deprivation, historical emergency hospital use, frailty indicators and a range of long-term conditions).

videos.title: MAN Huddle: Introducing Data Hazards -  07/09/22
videos.description:
Introducing Data Hazards – how can analysts and data scientists use Data Hazards in our day to day work?
This session is be run by Zoë Turner, data scientist in Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust.
08/09/22
    
If our profession of data analysts/data scientists in health and care is to be recognised for the power of good we can do then we must also be responsible for highlighting how our work can potentially cause harm; and that’s where Data Hazards can help to facilitate those discussions. The process of outlining Data Hazards was started by Natalie Zelenka and Nina Di Cara, who also run the Data Ethics Club, on their website which is open to contribution and released under an open licence to use. The hazards are visually depicted, like COSHH chemical hazards, and are a concise way of communicating and inviting opinions on projects. Whilst Natalie and Nina concentrated on the value of this to research, this short introduction in this week’s Huddle will attempt to show how analysts and data scientists can use the Data Hazards in our day to day work. Together we’ll consider a couple of case scenarios and discuss the benefits (or perhaps not!) of using something like Data Hazards labels regularly in our work. We’d be really interested to see what you think!

Recent analysis has found that demand for health and social care may not necessarily increase in line with an ageing population. Because older people may stay healthy for longer, or they may experience milder health conditions. The Health Economics Unit, with support from the REAL Centre, investigated whether this was the case in North West London.

In this Huddle we will cover:

Theories on whether an ageing population leads to higher lifetime health and social care spending
 
Introduction to Survival Analysis
 
Methodology for the North West London analysis
 
Results from our analysis
 
Recommendations and caveats

It would be useful but not essential to have some basic analytical skills to understand the technical elements of this huddle but everyone is very welcome!  After this session, you’ll have a good understanding of survival analysis, recent literature and a case study on the use of survival analysis

Your presenters will be Yihan Xu and Santosh Kumar (Health Economics Unit).

videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 20/10/22

MDSN Regional Analysis: What are the health implications of reduced access to care during the COVID 19 pandemic?

Project Lead, Paul Seamer (Strategy Unit) describes his approach and key findings for this important Midlands Decision Support Network (MDSN) Regional Analysis. The MDSN agrees an analytical work programme every year.  This is an annual programme of 3 projects determined by the network steering group and is focused on agreed network priorities. 

What are the health implications of reduced access to care during the COVID 19 pandemic?  Access to many forms of planned and unplanned healthcare reduced dramatically during the COVID-19 pandemic and associated lockdowns. 

The aims of this project were to investigate:
- The effect on health outcomes of changes in healthcare utilisation during the COVID-19 pandemic
- The actions available to health systems to mitigate these effects

This was done by:
- Exploring how the overall activity changed, by looking at the trends in activity levels for key services, for example, A&E visits, planned admissions, emergency admissions and primary care consultations
- In-depth analysis of unplanned emergency care to look for differences in current patterns of morbidity compared with pre-Covid
- A focused analysis of the impact of reduced access to care for diabetes patients
- Reviewing the implications for health care systems and identifying strategies and interventions to help health systems mitigate the negative effects

videos.title: MAN Huddle: INSIGHT 2022 The new Health Index - Midlands Focus - 01/12/22
videos.description:
MAN Huddle
INSIGHT 2022: Sam Booth (ONS) takes us through the new Health Index – Midlands focus

1st December 2022

Sam Booth, Lead Researcher (Integrated Care Systems and Health Index) joins the Huddle to tell us about the new Health Index.  Find out more about the Health Index and how it can support Integrated Care Systems (ICS) to achieve their purpose and maximising the impact of the index at a local level.

The Health Index for England is a new measure of the health of the nation. It uses a broad definition of health, including:
- health outcomes
- health-related behaviours and personal circumstances
- wider drivers of health that relate to the places where people live

The Health Index: 2015 to 2020  provides a systematic, independent view of health in England.  It can be used to compare health over time and across geographies. It gives a picture of health in its broadest sense, recognising the importance of health outcomes, risk factors and the social, economic, and environmental drivers which affect people’s lives. Data is published at local authority and integrated care system geographies as well as for regions and England as a whole.  A semi-automated online article, how health has changed in your local area, presents users with data and insights for their local area.

The session will cover:
- What the Health Index is
- Insights from the Health Index
- How to access and use the Health Index at a local level
- Next steps in development

This Huddle will be of interest to policy makers, commissioners and analysts who aim to use data and insights about their populations to improve health now and for the long term.

The Midlands Decision Support Network (MDSN) agrees an analytical work programme every year.  This is an annual programme of 3 significant projects determined by the network steering group and focused on agreed network priorities. This report is part for the 22/23 programme.

The number of diagnostic tests carried out in secondary care has increased substantially over the last two decades. An increase in diagnostic testing brings undoubted benefits. Yet, there has been limited consideration of the indirect effects of this growth.

Examples of the projects being developed in the Midlands System Dynamics Applied Learning Programme (Part 1)

Date: 06/04/2023

Over the last 6 months The Strategy Unit and Douglas McKelvie (Symmetric) have been running an applied learning programme in system dynamics. This is a method of simulation modelling that helps us look at the behaviour of systems over time and to ask ‘what if?’. The learning programme included both teaching sessions and project support. Twelve participants through the programme have been working individually or in pairs on projects using system dynamics to embed their learning and tackle real world strategic issues.

In this Huddle we will summarise the structure of the programme and describe two of the projects. 

The first looks at Community Mental Health future bed requirements, a work in progress from Sam Jones & Tom Jones from Staffordshire & Stoke ICB and North Staffs Combined Health respectively. Our second example is on the future need for care home places from Tracy Bennett & Jane Shaw from Shropshire Council.

We ask the audience to understand these projects are the participants’ first attempts at creating their own models using system dynamics, to appreciate the journey they have been on and to realise these are likely to still be developing.

videos.description:
NHS hip replacements and the inverse care law - with Steven Wyatt (Strategy Unit)

Date: 01/06/23

Fifty years ago, Julian-Tudor-Hart, a GP working in South Wales first described the Inverse Care Law.  
The law states that populations with the greatest need for a health service tend to be the least likely to receive it.  
Previous research has shown that the supply of elective hip replacements, a common and cost-effective means of improving hip function, follows the inverse care law.  

In this Midlands Analysts Huddle, Steven Wyatt, Head of Research and Policy at the Strategy Unit will talk about whether efforts to improve equity of access to hip replacements have paid off.

Date: 29th June 2023

NHS England’s Analysis and Insight for Finance team provide an overview of their overall approach and models for calculating fair shares which together distribute over a £100 billion in funding to ICBs. This will be followed by a more detailed look at how individual models are developed (e.g. variables, methods, QA), taking the General & Acute model as an example.

Supporting vulnerable patients and improving the management of long term conditions

Date:  27/07/23

- What are the barriers and facilitators impacting on vulnerable patient populations?
- How can we improve patient experiences and outcomes?

In May 2021 the Strategy Unit produced an analysis of ‘Socio-economic inequalities in access to planned hospital care’, this reported on socio-economic inequalities in the levels of primary and secondary care treatments received by patients for four conditions: COPD, Heart Failure, Hip Arthritis (OA Hip) and Cataracts. In the Black Country the most prominent inequality centered on the OA Hip pathway, in particular in relation to levels of Total Hip Replacement surgery (THR).

The Black Country Healthier Futures Academy set up a project, led by Rosalind Smithson (Principal Analyst – Qualitative Methods, Healthier Futures Academy, Black Country Integrated Care System) to explore patients’ experiences of the OA pathway, investigating what factors facilitated patients to gain appropriate support and what acted as a barrier. 15 in-depth interviews were conducted with patients at different stages in the pathway living in Sandwell or Walsall.  Two focus groups were also conducted with First Contact Practitioners (FCP) and Advanced Physiotherapists on their experiences of working with patients and of the system itself.

This session will give a brief overview of the Strategy Unit analysis (Steven Wyatt) before Rosalind Smithson’s presentation of the project findings and how these led to a series of applied pathway recommendations for improvement.  The results focus on pathway navigation, and how the existing pathway relies on patients successfully negotiating the pathway largely on their own.  In between touch points with medical professionals, patients had to manage their condition independently and co-ordinate the various aspects of their care. There were a number of system factors (e.g., the practice approach of health professionals, pathway processes, treatment criteria etc.,) which can support or create a barrier to patients directing and self-managing their condition, and patient factors (e.g., other health conditions, confidence, family support, etc.) that can support or act as a barrier.

MAN Huddle: 02/11/23
Understanding Waiting List Pressures (using queuing theory)

With Neil Walton who is a Professor in Operations Management at Durham University Business School.
Using queuing theory to understand the demand, queue size, waiting times, capacity requirements and trade-offs for different waiting lists.

NHS waiting lists currently sit at record lengths due to a combination of the immediate impact of the pandemic and, as well as, long-run pressures requiring investment on NHS resources. These factors have left managers and clinicians with increasingly complex decisions when scheduling elective operations. It is imperative that managers understand the basic dynamics, tradeoffs, and pressures when managing waiting lists.

Queueing theory is a key part of operational research, extensively used throughout manufacturing, retail, information technology and other sectors. This work provides an exposition of the theory of queues within the context of the current NHS backlog. With this information a manager will be able understand the demand, queue size, waiting times, capacity requirements and trade-offs for different waiting lists. We describe the metrics and a reporting system developed to understand waiting list pressures in a large NHS trust.

Our aim is to enable managers to better understand their waiting lists, to achieve targets and improve health outcomes.

Staff are released for a day a week from their usual role for 15 months to first undertake 6 months of training, and then supported by a community of over 300 modelling and data science experts to undertake a project that addresses an issue of importance for their organisation, immediately applying their new skills.  Previous HSMA projects have led to £multi-million new mental health, support for the COVID mass vaccination programme, transformative improvements to urgent care services and the formation of dedicated modelling and data science teams within trusts. videos.title: MAN Huddle: 21/03/24 The 85% bed occupancy fallacy
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 21/03/24
Topic: The 85% bed occupancy fallacy 
How useful is a bed occupancy target? 
With Nathan Proudlove, The University of Manchester

This talk is in some ways a companion piece to Prof Neil Wilson’s talk on waiting list pressures, which used some insights from queuing theory models to consider the size of a bed pool required to keep the risk (or proportion) of patients breaching some waiting time limit within some target value (Fong et al, 2022).

Analytical queuing theory models can give us quick, first-cut answers on a range of performance metrics, under certain conditions; more complex systems and contexts can be modelled (much more laboriously) by building computer simulations. 

A BMJ paper of a simple inpatient system (Bagust et al, 1999) was influential forming DH views on bed occupancy and management, but these were not well considered. 

In this talk we look at what queuing theory models tell us about the relationship between utilisation (e.g., bed occupancy) and waiting times, and reflect on the usefulness (or otherwise) of the policy of a target bed occupancy of e.g. 85%, as was prevalent in some DH guidance and trust policies some years ago. These models can give us further insights into things like the impact on performance of capacity carve out versus pooling (e.g., bed ring fencing vs pooling). 

The commonly used basic analytical queuing models (as above) require many assumptions for the maths to be tractable, including about the shape of the randomness in arrivals and service times (e.g. length of stay). This overlooks and hides the dramatic impact that the amount of variation (e.g., the standard deviation) has on system performance – and variation reduction is, of course, at the heart of improvement approaches such as lean an six sigma.

The final stage is an approximate queuing theory model that allows us to see this impact of variation explicitly; in fact we can see that system Performance (e.g. expected waiting time) is related to  Variation × Utilisation × service Time, the ‘VUT Relationship’. The size of the bed pool (i.e, the  amount of bed pooling) is also an input to the model. So, with this we can see, and approximately quantify, the power of and trade-offs between these key drivers of system performance.

The talk draws on material from Proudlove (2020) [also Proudlove (2023)]. Open access version of the paper:
www.researchgate.net/publication/335487564_The_85_bed_occupancy_fallacy_The_use_misuse_and_insights_of_queuing_theory 
and its appendix: www.researchgate.net/publication/376678922_Proudlove_2020_HSMR_bed_occupancy_fallacy_App_17docx

This analysis aims to identify clusters in practice staffing levels using routine general practice consultations and to assess distribution of clusters within practice deprivation quintiles.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: 08/08/24 Health inequalities in 2040: Current and future patterns in England
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 08/08/24
Topic: Health inequalities in 2040: Current and future patterns of inequalities in illness in England

With Ann Raymond, The Health Foundation

On current trends, health inequalities are projected to persist into the future. This has significant implications not just for population health but for labour supply and wider economic growth.

The existence of wide inequalities in health across England is well-documented. This Health Foundation research adds to this evidence on inequalities in self-reported health by describing current patterns and projecting future patterns of inequality in diagnosed illness across multiple conditions by deprivation.

They used the IMPACTNCD microsimulation model that simulates a close-to-reality synthetic population of adults in England from 2019 to 2040. This model combines individual-level data on demographics, health and mortality from linked administrative data for primary and secondary care with survey responses on individual-level risk factors and epidemiological evidence on the associations between risk factors and chronic illness.

Ann and colleagues used the Cambridge Multimorbidity Score (CMS) as our multimorbidity measure. This assigns a weight to 20 common long-term conditions based on individuals’ healthcare use and their likelihood of death. We further focus on “major illness” which corresponds to a CMS greater than 1.5.

In preliminary results, health inequalities are not projected to improve between 2019 and 2040. In 2019, the share of working age people living with major illness in the most deprived 10% of areas in England (14.6%) was more than double the rate seen in the least deprived 10% of areas (6.3%). In 2040, we project these rates to remain largely unchanged at 15.2% (13.0%, 17.6%) and 6.8% (5.4%, 9.1%) respectively.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: NHSquicker: Shaping Demand for Urgent Care Using Real-Time Data  - 31/10/24
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 31/10/24 
Topic: NHSquicker: Shaping Demand for Urgent Care Using Real-Time Data and Digital Nudges 
With Nav Mustafee, Professor of Operations Management and Analytics at the University of Exeter Business School

This research and impact work investigates whether indirect suggestions (nudges) can support patients needing urgent care to make more informed decisions about available healthcare choices. 
A nudge can be delivered using targeted adverts, mail campaigns, and, central to the theme of this research, through "digital" means using apps and wearables. 

https://nhsquicker.co.uk/ 

NHSquicker is a platform co-developed with the NHS Trusts in southwest England. It is designed to deliver nudges to inform patients of alternative locations for urgent care. NHSquicker comprises:

(a) a user-facing app that provides suggestions taking into account the live waiting time from Accident & Emergency (A&E) departments and Urgent Care Centres (UCC)/Minor Injury Units (MIU)/Walk-in Centres (WICs), also factoring the travel time; 
(b) the platform backend that receives real-time feeds and allows for easy integration of new feeds from Trusts that join the initiative. 

The app helps patients make informed decisions, for example, whether they visit a facility which may be nearer to them but with a long waiting time or travel to an alternative location that is further away but with a shorter waiting time. 
An evaluation framework captures evidence of impact and triangulate findings from patient questionnaires, secondary data analysis and app analytics. 

Our study has shown the potential of NHSquicker to shape demand for urgent care by reducing A&E visits from low-acuity attendees and helping redirect patients to UCC/MIU/WICs and other healthcare facilities.
 A sustained communication effort by the NHS will further increase patients' adoption of NHSquicker (or other such real-time solutions) and help realise further benefits for the Trusts.
The NHSquicker project was initiated in 2017 at the University of Exeter Business School. Over the years, the network has grown. It currently covers all urgent care facilities in Devon, Cornwall and Somerset. It received funding from NHS Devon ICB in September 2023.  

Meet our presenter: Navonil (Nav) Mustafee is a Professor of Operations Management and Analytics at the University of Exeter Business School. His research focuses on Modelling & Simulation methodologies and their application in Healthcare Operations Management, Supply Chain, Sustainability and the Circular Economy. 
Nav is the joint editor-in-chief of the Journal of Simulation (UK OR Society journal) and associate editor of Health Systems and Simulation: The Transactions of the SCS.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: COMPLEX-IT: Enabling Non-Experts to Leverage Advanced Computational Modelling - 12/12/24
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 12/12/24
Topic: COMPLEX-IT: Enabling Non-Experts to Leverage Advanced Computational Modelling for Policy Evaluation and Decision Making

With Brian Castellani, PhD. FAcSS, Professor of Social and Public Health, Director, Research Methods Centre, Co-Director, Wolfson Research Institute for Health and Wellbeing, Durham University, UK; Adjunct Professor of Psychiatry, Northeastern Ohio Medical University, US and Lasse Gerrits, Professor and Academic Director, Institute for Housing and Urban Development Studies, Erasmus University Rotterdam, the Netherlands

Over the past decade, computational methods for decision support - ranging from simulation and machine learning to network analysis and systems mapping—have advanced significantly. However, the challenge remains in making these tools accessible to non-experts, particularly those involved in healthcare research, strategy, and policy evaluation. This methods session addresses that need. 
Brian introduces COMPLEX-IT, a free, intuitive R-platform designed to equip non-experts with cutting-edge tools in machine learning, data visualization, participatory systems mapping, network analysis, simulation, data forecasting, and cluster analysis. Through hands-on exploration of a real-world dataset, participants will gain a step-by-step understanding of how to use COMPLEX-IT to enhance decision making in healthcare. By the session’s conclusion, attendees will leave with a powerful, practical platform they can readily apply to their own research and policy evaluation efforts. 
For more, see https://www.complex-it-data.org/

This session is for anyone keen to learn more about how to use computational methods (e.g., AI, networks, simulation, systems mapping and machine learning) in their healthcare work or research.

Process Mining in Healthcare – Opportunities and Challenges 
With Owen Johnson, Director of Impact, School of Computer Science, University of Leeds

Find out more about the opportunities and challenges for using Process Mining in healthcare.
The NHS needs shorter waiting lists and faster, better, more effective care pathways. We can and should be using NHS data to understand the options for improvement but data mining does not have the answers, NHS data analysts and data scientists need to understand process mining and use it as part of their analytics tool set. This talk introduces process mining with examples of how it has helped NHS case studies.

A simple approach to process mining is introduced along with an overview of the ClearPath method and a discussion on the unique challenges and opportunities ahead. The talk ends with a discussion on how to implement process mining within local practice with signposting to resources that will help.

videos.title: MAN: Public expenditure in the last year of life Nuffield Trust & Health Economics Unit - 20/02/2025
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 20/02/2025
Topic: Public expenditure in the last year of life - Nuffield Trust & Health Economics Unit
With Lisa Cummins and Gayathri Kumar, Health Economics Unit

Supporting people at the end of life is a crucially important element of public spending, yet there is remarkably little evidence available on how much money is being spent on it, and what that money goes on. The Nuffield Trust and the Health Economics Unit were commissioned by Marie Curie to estimate the range of public expenditure that supports the care of people in their last year, to help inform national and local funding decisions to improve services for people at the end of life.
•  Around 650,000 adults die each year in the UK, with one in six dying in poverty. We know that the care and support people receive from publicly funded services greatly influences the quality of their last year of life – yet very little is known about the cost of the care and support they receive.
• To address this gap, and to help inform decision makers on the best possible use of funding, the Health Economics Unit (HEU), in collaboration with the Nuffield Trust, were commissioned by Marie Curie to estimate how much the UK spends on people in the last year of life.
"We undertook analysis of published data and statistics and extensive stakeholder engagement to estimate how much health care, social care and social security funding was spent on people in their last year of life across all four nations of the United Kingdom (UK) in 2022. We also performed sensitivity analysis to assess uncertainty in our estimates."

videos.title: MAN Huddle: 03/04/2025 Toy Model for risk stratification and healthcare needs in the future
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 03/04/2025
Topics:
Toy models – Complex problems in small packages! and 
How much healthcare will our population need in five, ten, 20 years' time?”

With Andy Hood and Lucy Morgan, and Paul Seamer, from the Strategy Unit https://www.strategyunitwm.nhs.uk

Toy models – Complex problems in small packages!

Often analysts find themselves in situations having to describe complex theories and their intended or unintended consequences to decision-makers but with data itself that is complicated or that overwhelms the theory. Toy models provide a way of distilling key mathematical concepts on a given topic or issue and providing simple data and a platform on which to explore, test and visualise them. The Strategy Unit (SU), funded through the New Hospitals Programme (NHP) is developing a series of toy models that explore risk stratification cost effectiveness, bed pooling & identifying bottle necks that impact patient flow and left-shift. These tools, it is hoped, will allow analysts, decision-makers, trainers and students to explore these concepts in a digestible way and gauge the high-level impacts of changing approaches before doing so at scale. In this bite-size session we will be introducing and demonstrating the Risk Stratification toy model app and trailing the other upcoming toy models which will all be made publicly available. 
Aimed predominantly at analysts, this session will (hopefully) introduce the key concepts in risk stratification implementation; demonstrate the impacts of changing any of these features; provide links to freely access this tool and describe plans for similar upcoming and future tools.

21:37 How much healthcare will our population need in five, ten, 20 years' time?

At a previous huddle the Strategy Unit shared a beta version of a new interactive tool that showed how population aging, and other demographic changes will impact the future need for different types of hospital services across local areas.
During the earlier huddle session, we asked for volunteers to help with usability testing. A number of people kindly volunteered to review the tool and provided helpful feedback. We are now ready to officially launch the tool. This short session will include a demo of the new tool, a reminder of the themes it addresses, and an opportunity to ask questions.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: 26/05/25
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 26/05/25
Topic: Humans, AI and the Importance of Data Literacy’
With Dan Isaac, Data Literacy & Training Lead, Exeter University

Everyone is talking about AI, but people aren’t talking about the humans that use AI and the data that fuels it. In this talk, Dan aims to correct that by discussing:

The role of humans in evaluating AI
• Why AI tools and their human users should be evaluated as a singular system of distributed cognition
• The importance of prompt engineering
• Should we trust AI?
 AI’s data problem
• "Garbage In, Garbage Out": AI will provide poor outputs unless it is fed from good data.
• How can we define 'good' data?
• Understanding Availability Bias for humans and AI
• The data challenge faced by 'legacy' organisation
• The knowledge gap between AI/Data Professionals and Business Leaders
 Why humans need data literacy
• What is Data Literacy?
• Always asking "What does the data tell us?" when making a decision
• Data literacy is not intuitive and must be learned

Dan Isaac is the Data Literacy & Training Lead at the University of Exeter and a specialist in Data Visualisation, with a particular interest in the psychology behind effective data communication. Based at the University of Exeter, Dan has been delivering Data Visualisation training since 2013 and also teaching on the MSc Business Analytics programme at the University’s Business School.

Topic: 'Rules of Thumb' for assessing the quality of analysis
With Fraser Battye (Strategy Unit) and Danielle Jefferies (The Kings Fund)

How do you assess the quality of analytical work? 
When you first receive a report, what are the first signs and signals you are looking for? 
The author(s)? The layout? The methods? Data sources? Drafting? 
And - of all the quick tests of quality you are performing - could a non-analyst be primed to see the same things? 
Are there any 'rules of thumb' that non-analysts could use to assess the likely quality of analytical work? 

At this huddle, we will examine these questions with Fraser Battye (Head of Policy, Strategy Unit) and Danielle Jefferies (Analyst at the Kings Fund). They will present the results of a project, which drew on interviews with senior analysts, and suggest that there are pointers which non-analysts could use to get a first-approximation assessment of analytical quality.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: Simplifying statistical process control with I-prime charts - 07/08/2025
videos.description:
MAN Huddle - 07/08/2025
Topic: Simplifying statistical process control with I-prime charts
With

In this Huddle, you will be introduced to the I-prime (I') chart – a new and improved SPC tool that retains the simplicity of the I chart while addressing its limitations. It handles both measurement and count data, adapts to varying subgroup sizes, and holds the potential to replace other common SPC charts.

Target audience: The webinar is intended for analysts and practitioners involved in healthcare quality control and improvement. Prior experience with SPC methodology and programming in R will be beneficial but not essential.  If this isn't you, you are still very welcome to come along and learn a bit more about SPC charts and about what can be achieved from programming in R. 

Aims: After the session you will:
• understand the theory behind I' charts,
• know when – and when not – to use I' charts as alternatives to traditional SPC charts, and
• be able to construct I' charts using R.

Preparations and materials: No preparation is required to participate in the webinar. However, if you would like to refresh your understanding of basic SPC theory and practice, we recommend browsing Part 1 of our work-in-progress book:

• Anhøj & Mohammed (2025): Mastering Statistical Process Control Charts in Healthcare. A book under development. https://anhoej.github.io/spc4hc/

If you want a head start on the theory behind I' charts, we recommend reading Taylor's original paper:
• Taylor (2018): Normalized Individuals Control Chart. The original article introducing I' charts.
https://variation.com/normalized-individuals-control-chart/

Also, you may wish to install and familiarise yourself with pbcharts, an R package currently in development:
• Anhøj (2025): Process Behaviour Charts. Yet another R package for making SPC charts:
devtools::install_github("anhoej/pbcharts")
https://github.com/anhoej/pbcharts

• Sizing new hospitals so they are fit for purpose
• Supporting the ‘left shift’ by identifying care that could be prevented or delivered in homes and communities

During the session we will explore:

MAN Huddle: 27/11/25
Topic: The Networked Data Lab - What can linked data tell us about the elective care waiting list?
With Tom Prendergast, Senior Data Analyst (The Health Foundation), 
Anna Palczewska, Senior Data Scientist and Josh Elvidge-Murgatroyd, Data Engineer/ Analyst (West Yorkshire ICB)

Join this Huddle to find out what really happens while people wait for elective care? Learn about uncovering inequalities, patient journeys and the realities of working with the WLMDS.

Through the Health Foundation’s Networked Data Lab, analytical teams in four areas of the UK (West Yorkshire, Cheshire and Merseyside, North West London, and Grampian) have linked data on elective waiting times to primary and secondary healthcare datasets to examine inequalities in waiting times and the impact of waiting on health.

In this talk, Tom Prendergast, Senior Data Analyst (The Health Foundation), Anna Palczewska, Senior Data Scientist and Josh Elvidge-Murgatroyd, Data Engineer/ Analyst (West Yorkshire ICB), will be discussing what they learned from this research and the many challenges of examining the elective waiting list using linked data. 

What you will learn:
How waiting times for care and experiences while on the waiting list, vary between population groups; how much and what kinds of other healthcare do people use while waiting for and recovering from elective care; challenges of working with the WLMDS and how some of these can be overcome.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: From hospital to community: shifting care or swimming uphill? -  08/01/2026
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 08/01/2026
Topic: From hospital to community: shifting care or swimming uphill?
With Fraser Battye, Head of Policy at the Strategy Unit

The shift from hospital to community is one of the three main aims of current health policy. This is not new. Indeed, the desire for a less hospital-centric health and care system has been a fairly consistent aim for several decades.

Why has progress proved so elusive? And what will current efforts – on neighbourhood health for example – have to contend with if they are to be successful?

Fraser Battye, Head of Policy at the Strategy Unit, will examine these questions. He will present the hopeful pessimist’s view: that a more community-focused care system is desirable, but that achieving it will be like swimming uphill. As well as outlining broad, secular trends, Fraser will point to elements where analytical skills are needed.

Shifting care from hospital to community is a core ambition of current health policy, but understanding where there may be genuine opportunities for change - and how big they are - remains challenging.

This session will:

videos.title: MAN: Using data to inform the role of a specialist children's hospital in the left shift - 19/02/26
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 19/02/2026
Topic: Using data to inform the role of a specialist children's hospital in the left shift 
With Izaak Gilchrist. Senior Analyst at Edge Health https://www.linkedin.com/in/izaak-gilchrist/

As healthcare systems transition toward neighbourhood-based care, specialist children’s hospitals must define their role. This session presents a deep-dive analysis into the "Left Shift, the movement of care from acute hospital beds into the community.

In this Huddle I will be joined by Izaak Gilchrist who is a Senior Analyst at Edge Health and who is in the Analytics Team at the Children's Hospital Alliance (CHA) which is a national network of specialist NHS trusts working together to improve the quality, access and experience of hospital care for children and families.

Izaak will share a robust methodology for identifying potentially "divertible" patient cohorts, revealing that a percentage of all non-elective admissions across the CHA Trusts could be effectively managed in non-acute settings. By breaking down the data by age, diagnosis, and cost, this presentation provides a roadmap for how specialist trusts can lead the design of community-based services rather than simply reacting to them.

What you will learn:
·         The Divertibility Framework: A methodology for identifying which patient cohorts (e.g., respiratory, seizure-related) are "primed" for community care.
·         The Scale of Impact: An analysis of the annual admissions that could be diverted and the millions of pounds in variable costs associated with them.
·         Strategic Intervention and "Influencing the Money"

Who is this session for?
·         Data Analysts
·         Service Planners & Commissioners: To understand where to allocate resources based on specialist trends.
·         Integrated Care Board (ICB) Leads: To see how specialist hospitals fit into the broader "Neighbourhood" strategy.
·         Clinical Leads: To understand how pathways may be redesigned outside the hospital walls.
·         Operational Managers: To prepare for the potential shift in patient volume and the changing role of hospital outpatient services.

videos.title: MAN: Building an open source model to understand future demand in CKD/KRT pathways - 05/03/2026
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 05/03/2026
Topic: Building an open source model to understand future demand in CKD/KRT pathways
with Strategy Unit colleagues 

In this session we will introduce our renal demand and capacity model (Kidney-SCOPE) and how we are developing it using the principles of open-science.

Kidney-SCOPE is a hybrid simulation model for use in understanding the required capacity for renal services in the future under no-change and intervention scenarios. The model is novel in its use of system dynamics (SD) to represent the progression of (CKD) combined with the use of discrete event simulation (DES) to mimic patient pathways in kidney replacement therapy (KRT). The combination of models allows us to investigate the impact of interventions in both the upstream (i.e. prevention and new medications) and downstream (i.e. increase in home dialysis) models.

Since October 2025 we have been redeveloping the original DES component of Kidney-SCOPE to make it available open-source using the simPy package in Python. We would like to use this session to reflect upon what we've learnt from the process and share what has and hasn't worked well.

Disclaimer - we have now released version 1 of the model on GitHub but it is still under development as we receive feedback from the renal centres we're working with.

What you will learn:
• about hybrid simulation modelling for chronic conditions
• the approach from commercial to open-source modelling

Who is this session for?
• Anyone with an interest in simulation, it won't be too technical so this should be of interest to a broad audience which could include commissioners, clinicians and any decision-makers who are interested in this topic
• Anyone specifically interested in open-source modelling and inter-disciplinary working

videos.title: MAN Huddle: The Art of the Adjacent Possible - 28/05/2026
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 28/05/2026
Topic: The Art of the Adjacent Possible *
With Neil Pettinger, Kurtosis

During this Huddle Neil will explore if we can find data clues within existing practice that suggest improvements in patient flow might be more within our grasp than we think?

Patient flow continues to be a problem for acute hospitals. And we are all aware that unless we can do something remarkable and sustainable to improve bed availability, it will continue to be a problem. But the directorates and specialties that manage hospital beds do not usually have ready access to data that would enable them to identify possibilities for improvement.

This talk proposes a way of presenting flow metrics to inpatient directorates and specialties so that managers and clinicians can tap into the potential of internal benchmarking – what Neil is calling ‘the adjacent possible’* – in order to identify those possibilities for improvement.

This is an exploratory session, and Neil will be actively inviting feedback on whether this approach feels credible, useful and workable in practice.

* “What is actual now enables what is next possible: the adjacent possible.” -Stuart Kauffman

videos.title: MAN Huddle: A deeper look at failure demand in healthcare - 11/06/26
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 11/06/26
Topic: A deeper look at failure demand in healthcare
With Alison Turner, Head of Knowledge Mobilisation, The Strategy Unit

In this Huddle, Alison Turner, Head of Knowledge Mobilisation, will take a deeper, more analyst-focused look at failure demand in healthcare, following the broader Strategy Unit webinar on the same topic.

Failure demand is the work created when people’s needs are not met effectively first time - for example, repeated contacts, avoidable follow-up activity, or demand generated by delays and fragmented care. One of the challenges is that this work can often appear in data as if it were productive output.

Alison will introduce the key concepts, share an emerging typology of failure demand, and explore how analysts might begin to recognise it in their own datasets. The session will also reflect on the hidden costs for patients, carers and staff, and ask what it would mean to bring this perspective more explicitly into analytical work.

This will be a reflective and participative session, with opportunities to test ideas and connect them to your own experience.

Who is this session for?
This Huddle will be useful for anyone working with demand, productivity, performance or improvement data - especially analysts, planners, improvement leads and decision-makers curious about how failure demand might show up in practice.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: Do we need more hospital beds? - 06/08/2026
videos.description:
MAN Huddle: 06/08/2026
Topic: Do we need more hospital beds? 
With Lucy Morgan, Head of Analytics and Modelling at the Strategy Unit

For more than 30 years, hospital admissions have risen while bed numbers have fallen. A major reason this has been possible is the remarkable reduction in average length of stay - from around 8.5 days in 1994 to approximately 2.6 days today.

But length of stay is now levelling off and may be approaching its practical limit. If admissions continue to grow, what might this mean for future hospital capacity?

In this Huddle I’m joined by, Lucy Morgan, Head of Analytics and Modelling at the Strategy Unit, who will introduce the interactive app Do we need more hospital beds?

The app allows users to explore more than 30 years of national trends and test assumptions about admissions, length of stay, occupancy and future bed requirements.

Lucy will show how it can be used to:
• understand the trends that have shaped hospital capacity 
• examine how changes in admissions could affect future bed needs 
• explore how much activity different levels of bed capacity could support 
• test what may be reasonable to assume about future length of stay and occupancy 
• support better conversations about demand, capacity and hospital planning 

The model is deliberately simple, but it highlights an increasingly urgent challenge. If length of stay cannot continue to fall at the same rate, and hospital capacity cannot expand significantly, reducing growth in admissions becomes increasingly important.

This session will be relevant to analysts, commissioners, hospital planners, clinicians, decision-makers and anyone interested in the future of hospital care. No specialist modelling knowledge is required.

videos.title: MAN Huddle: Why Hospital Admission Avoidance Schemes May Not Reduce Bed Occupancy - 20/08/2026
videos.description:
MAN Huddle:  - 20/08/2026

Topic: Hospital Admission Thresholds, the Left Shift, and Why Admission Avoidance Schemes May Not Reduce Bed Occupancy

With Andrew Jones and Steven Wyatt, The Strategy Unit 

If admission avoidance and left shift successfully free up hospital beds… what stops those beds simply filling up again?

Every patient attending an Emergency Department effectively encounters a threshold for admission. Clinical need is obviously central to that decision, but other factors can also play a part - including available hospital capacity and the alternatives to hospital care. So, if better community and neighbourhood services release hospital capacity, could the threshold for admission quietly fall? And if it does, might some of the capacity created through left shift simply be absorbed by patients who would previously not have been admitted?

At the Huddle, I’ll be joined by my Strategy Unit colleagues Andrew Jones and Steven Wyatt, who have been exploring exactly this.

They’ll explain the idea of an admission threshold, demystify casemix-adjusted odds of admission, show what they have found when looking at changes over time, and explore whether admission thresholds could potentially be monitored using routinely collected ED data.

It should be a really interesting mix of analysis, methods and a much bigger question about how we make left shift work in practice.

With Fraser Battye and Charles Tallack 

Fraser Battye and Charles Tallack will explore the opportunities being created for analysts by strategic commissioning and other developments across health and care.

Analysis is increasingly being asked to help answer some fundamental questions: What should priorities be, given the needs of the population? How can limited resources be used to best effect? What outcomes result from changes in service provision?

In principle, analysis is looking less ‘nice to have’ and more ‘absolutely fundamental’. But what needs to be true for that to happen in practice – and what do analysts and their organisations need to do to make it a reality?
